skillChecks.success: The character offers Guh something she has never tasted — magical food, exotic cuisine, or an incredibly persuasive description of a feast beyond her imagination. Combined with an offering of actual food (or creative use of Prestidigitation to enhance mundane food), Guh is so delighted that she grants the party one request. If they ask for the conch, she is confused but agrees — she did not even know it was there.
skillChecks.failure: Guh is unimpressed. 'Guh has eaten EVERYTHING. You bring... nothing new. Nothing WORTHY.' She hurls a chunk of debris at the party as a warning shot.

skillChecks.success: The character confronts Guh with her worst fear: 'You cannot stand. You cannot run. You cannot fight. Every giant in this steading could walk away, and you would starve, alone, on your throne of garbage.' Guh's composure shatters. She begins to cry — enormous, blubbery sobs that shake the building — and surrenders. She tells the goblins to give the party whatever they want, including the conch.
skillChecks.failure: Guh's fear transforms into rage. She hurls debris at the character with terrifying accuracy and orders her guards to attack. Combat begins with Guh having already acted (thrown debris, +8, 3d10+5).

skillChecks.success: The character spots the distinctive spiral shape of the Conch of Teleportation wedged beneath the base of Guh's throne platform, partially buried in treasure and debris.
skillChecks.failure: The conch is not visible. It requires excavating the base of the throne (10 minutes, or DC 20 Athletics to pull free under pressure) to find.

skillChecks.success: The character destroys a critical load-bearing support, causing a section of the roof to collapse on Guh. 6d10 bludgeoning damage, DC 16 Dex save for half — but Guh cannot make the save because she cannot move. The party must make DC 14 Dex saves to avoid the same collapse.
skillChecks.failure: The support cracks but holds. The attempt alerts everyone in the room to the character's intent.

enemies: Chief Guh (modified Hill Giant: HP 145, AC 12 — too fat for proper armor, immobile — speed 0, cannot be moved. Attacks: Hurl Debris +8, range 60/240, 3d10+5 bludgeoning; Thunderous Bellow recharge 5-6, bonus action, 30-ft cone, DC 14 Constitution save or stunned until end of next turn and deafened for 1 minute; Sweeping Arm +8, reach 10 ft, 2d8+5 bludgeoning and DC 14 Strength save or pushed 10 ft and knocked prone)
2 Hill Giant Bodyguards (CR 5, HP 105 each, AC 13)
8 Goblin Attendants (CR 1/4, HP 7 each, AC 15 — they flee after round 1 unless the goblin shaman is alive, in which case they fight fanatically)
1 Goblin Shaman (if not killed at the shrine: CR 1, HP 21, AC 17, Bane and Inflict Wounds 1/day each)
combatEncounters.tactics: Chief Guh cannot move from her throne. She uses Hurl Debris every round against the most dangerous-looking enemy, prioritizing spellcasters. She uses Thunderous Bellow when 2+ enemies are within the cone. Her Sweeping Arm attacks anything that comes within 10 feet. The hill giant bodyguards position themselves to intercept melee attackers, fighting aggressively and prioritizing anyone heading toward Guh's throne base (where the conch is). The goblin attendants scatter after the first round of combat, but if the shaman is alive, he rallies them to harass the party's backline with hit-and-run dagger attacks. If both bodyguards fall, Guh's composure breaks — she begins hurling debris wildly (disadvantage on attacks) and screaming for help. If the building is sabotaged and begins collapsing, ALL creatures in the room must deal with falling debris (2d6 bludgeoning per round, DC 13 Dex save to avoid) — this affects the giants much more than the smaller party members. If Guh is reduced to 50 HP or below, she surrenders, weeping and begging for food.
combatEncounters.terrain: The throne room is 80 ft across with a 20-ft ceiling. Guh's throne platform is in the center, 10 ft high and 30 ft wide, accessible by crude log ramps on two sides. The floor is covered in debris, bones, and food scraps (difficult terrain throughout). Six log pillars support the roof (AC 15, HP 40; destroying 3+ collapses the roof). Piles of debris around the room provide half cover. The base of the throne is buried in treasure and refuse — accessing the conch requires being within 5 ft of the throne base. Guh has line of sight to the entire room from her elevated position. A ragged hole in the wall on the east side provides an emergency exit — a 30-ft drop to the muddy slope outside (DC 14 Acrobatics to land without damage, or 3d6 bludgeoning).

scenes.roleplayNotes: This is the climactic scene and should feel appropriately epic and grotesque. Chief Guh is simultaneously terrifying, pitiable, and absurd — a creature that pursued power through the only lens she understood (eating) and became a prisoner of her own success. The DM should play her as genuinely dangerous (her attacks hit HARD) but also as a tragic figure. She truly believes that being the fattest giant will make her the most powerful, because she cannot imagine any other form of strength. If the party negotiates, her delight at new food is childlike and genuine. If they intimidate her, her fear is real and raw. If they fight, her rage is the desperate fury of a creature that knows it cannot flee. The conch discovery should feel like a major plot revelation — it is clearly of storm giant origin, far more sophisticated than anything in the steading, and it hums with teleportation magic. A DC 14 Arcana check reveals it transports the user to Maelstrom, the undersea court of the storm giants. This is the thread that leads to the larger Storm King's Thunder campaign. After the encounter, the steading's remaining inhabitants (goblins, ogres) scatter without Guh's leadership. The slaves are freed. The Feast Trail ends. The party has dealt with the hill giant threat and gained a crucial artifact that connects to the storm giant court.
loot: Conch of Teleportation (plot item — transports the party to Maelstrom, the storm giant court; single use, but re-charges after a tenday)
Javelin of Lightning (rare, requires attunement — found in Guh's treasure hoard, stolen from an adventurer)
Gauntlets of Ogre Power (uncommon, requires attunement — worn by Guh as 'bracelets,' set the wearer's Strength to 19)

Guh's treasure hoard: 450 gp, 1,200 sp, 3,000 cp (all pressed into the filth and requiring 30 minutes to fully excavate), a gold-and-ruby necklace worth 250 gp, a silver hand mirror worth 75 gp, a set of masterwork thieves' tools worth 100 gp, and a cracked sending stone (its partner is held by another hill giant chief in the Spine of the World — plot hook)
From the bodyguards: 2 greatclubs, 4d10 gp each, crude iron armbands worth 15 gp each

Refugee network — the displaced farmers and merchants the party helped spread word of their deeds, granting advantage on Charisma checks in Sword Coast settlements

dmTips: Scale is everything in this scenario. Constantly remind players how BIG everything is when dealing with giants. A hill giant's footprint is 3 feet across. Their clubs are bigger than a human. Their voices shake the ground. The party should feel small and clever, relying on tactics, terrain, and teamwork rather than brute force.

Grudd Haug should feel disgusting. Lean into the sensory details: the smell, the sounds of eating, the refuse and decay everywhere. This is not a clean dungeon — it is a living, breathing, rotting thing built by creatures with no concept of sanitation. Players should feel viscerally uncomfortable.

Chief Guh is the emotional core of the scenario. Play her as both threatening and pathetic. She is dangerous — her thrown debris can one-shot a wizard — but she is also a creature trapped by her own delusion. The best outcomes involve the party recognizing both aspects.

The scenario rewards preparation. Parties that gather intelligence in Act 2 (from Tilda, Moog, Gurrash, captured goblins) have dramatically easier options in Act 3. If the party rushes to the steading without scouting, the frontal assault is doable but costly. Make sure Act 2 feels rewarding, not like filler.

Track alarm status in the steading carefully. A stealthy party can bypass most encounters and reach Guh with full resources. A loud party fights through everything and arrives at the boss fight depleted. Both are valid play styles, but the difficulty should feel consistent with the party's choices.
